## Carburettor Most BTC Riva 50 scooters from 2015 onwards are fitted with a **CVK18** constant velocity (CV) carburettor. Earlier models used a simpler **PZ18** slide carburettor. The CVK18 has a vacuum-operated slide and is generally more tolerant of altitude variation; the PZ18 is simpler and easier to rebuild. Standard jet sizes on the CVK18 for UK/Western Europe sea-level use: - **Main jet:** 75 (or 78 for some batches) — M5 × 0.8 thread - **Pilot/slow jet:** 38 or 40 - **Needle clip position:** Middle groove (groove 3 of 5) - **Air/fuel mixture screw (pre-set):** 2.0 turns out from gently seated � **Jetting note:** The Riva 50 is a restricted moped. Some owners fit a 35 mm exhaust restrictor insert and a small air-box restrictor at factory. These reduce power and can cause rich running at idle. ## Known Issues & Common Repairs ### Cold-Start Problems The most frequently reported issue on Dutch scooter forums is difficulty starting in cold or damp weather. The root causes are typically the **auto-choke thermostatic element** becoming sluggish in temperatures below 5°C, a partially blocked pilot jet, or a slightly low float level. See the [GY6 Carburetor Adjustment Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-adjustment-guide.html) and [GY6 No-Start Troubleshooting](/diagnostics/gy6-no-start-troubleshooting.html) for systematic diagnosis. ### Carburetor Type La Souris Sourini and City S carbureted models typically use a **Rongmao** or **Keihin PD18J clone** carburetor. Pilot jet size is typically `35`–`38` and main jet is typically `72`–`78` for the restricted 25 km/h snorfiets version. ## Lighting All La Souris City models have conventional halogen bulbs accessible through an access flap behind the headlamp — no special tools required for bulb replacement. City S models from 2019 onwards may have LED daytime running lights combined with halogen low beam. ## Parts Interchangeability The La Souris Sourini and City S share the GY6 platform with several other European-market Chinese scooters. The following models are mechanically similar and share most engine and drivetrain parts: - **BTC Riva** (same engine, same CVT belt, same GY6 carburetor) - **AGM VX50** - **Senzo Rivalux** - **GTS Toscana** - Generic Chinese 50cc scooters marketed under many brand names Body panels, headlamp units, mirrors, and instruments are **not** interchangeable between these brands — each has its own styling. Engine internals (pistons, camshafts, valves, bearings, seals), CVT components (rollers, belt, variator), and electrical components (CDI, rectifier, ignition coil) are largely interchangeable as they all derive from the same GY6 platform. � **Parts sourcing tip:** In the Netherlands and Belgium, [chinascooteronderdelen.nl](https://en.chinascooteronderdelen.nl/product-category/scooter-parts/parts-btc-agm-iva-senzo-la-souris/) specifically stocks parts for La Souris, BTC Riva, AGM, and Senzo models. ## Engine Oil — Checking & Changing The ZIP uses a dipstick on the right crankcase cover (no drain-plug sight glass). To check the level correctly: 1. Park the scooter on level ground on the centre stand. 2. Remove the dipstick, wipe it clean, reinsert it fully (screw in tightly), then remove it again to read the level. 3. The oil level must be between the MIN and MAX marks. Do not overfill — excess oil causes foaming and oil consumption. 4. To drain, unscrew the drain plug at the bottom of the crankcase. Torque to **25–28 Nm** on refitting. 5. Fill with approximately **850 cm³** of SELENIA HI SCOOTER 4Tech or equivalent SAE 5W-40 synthetic meeting JASO MA. ## Rear Hub Oil — Checking & Changing 1. Park on the centre stand on level ground. 2. Unscrew the dipstick (cap A), wipe dry, reinsert fully, then remove and check level is between the 2nd and 3rd notches from the bottom (MIN to MAX). 3. To change: remove the oil fill cap/dipstick and unscrew the drain cap (B). Drain fully. 4. Refit drain cap and fill with approximately **80 cm³** of AGIP ROTRA 80W-90 (SAE 80W/90, API GL3). 5. Hub oil must be changed at every 1,000 km or 4 months (whichever comes first) during the initial break-in period. ## Air Filter — Cleaning Procedure 1. Undo the 6 fixing screws and remove the air cleaner cover. 2. Extract the foam sponge filter element. 3. Wash with water and shampoo (household washing-up liquid is acceptable). 4. Rinse thoroughly, then dry with a clean cloth — do not wring or compress the sponge. 5. Soak the sponge in a 50/50 mixture of Selenia Air Filter Oil and unleaded petrol. 6. Allow to drip dry on a clean cloth, then gently squeeze by hand to remove excess oil without distorting the sponge. 7. Refit. Clean more frequently than the service schedule when riding on dusty roads. ️ **Never run without air filter:** Operating the engine with a missing or damaged air filter allows unfiltered air and dust to enter the cylinder, causing accelerated bore and piston ring wear. ## Common Issues & Known Faults - **Excessive fuel consumption:** Most commonly caused by a blocked air filter restricting airflow (engine runs rich), a stuck automatic cold-start (choke) device, loose main or pilot jets, or an incorrect float level in the KEIHIN carburettor. Clean the air filter and check the starter device mechanically before disassembling the carburettor. - **Drive belt slipping or glazing:** In urban stop-start use the drive belt can glaze before reaching its measured wear limit. If acceleration feels weak but the engine revs freely, inspect the belt surface for glazing and the clutch shoes for oil contamination. - **CVT roller flat-spotting:** The variator rollers develop flat spots over distance, causing a harsh, stepped sensation during acceleration and a top-speed reduction. Inspect at every 6,000 km service; replace as a complete set — never mix old and new rollers. - **Rear wheel spinning at idle:** Indicates idle speed set too high, or a faulty clutch with grease-contaminated friction masses. Verify idle is at 1,500 ± 150 rpm and inspect clutch masses for contamination. - **Front brake spongy feel:** Air in the hydraulic circuit. Bleed the front brake circuit using DOT 4 fluid; bleed valve torque is 8–12 Nm. - **Oil weeping from crankcase joint:** Crankcase half union screws (8–10 Nm) may need checking for torque and gasket condition if oil weeps from the centre joint. ## Service Manual & Documentation Resources - [ManualsLib — Piaggio ZIP manuals (PDF)](https://www.manualslib.com/brand/piaggio/zip/) - [Carl Salter — Free Piaggio/Vespa Workshop Manuals](https://www.carlsalter.com/piaggio-vespa-service-manuals.asp) - [Modern Vespa Forum — Workshop Manuals Wiki](https://www.modernvespa.com/forum/wiki-workshop-manuals) - [Piaggio official website](https://www.piaggio.com) — contact authorised dealer for current service documentation � **50cc maintenance:** Engine oil, rear hub oil, brake fluid, air filter, and scheduled service intervals are identical for both variants. The carburettor on the 50cc (KEIHIN CVK Ø 18 mm) uses the same cleaning and float-adjustment procedure as described for the 100cc unit, but jets and needle are not interchangeable between variants. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; The carburetor needle controls how much fuel mixes with air during the **mid-throttle range** (roughly 25%–75% open). When it is set too high, the mixture becomes too rich and the engine runs sluggishly, smokes black, and smells of unburnt fuel. When it is set too low, the mixture becomes too lean and the engine hesitates, surges, or overheats. Adjusting the needle is free, takes under an hour, and requires no special tools — making it one of the most rewarding first tuning jobs for any beginner. ️ **Fire safety — read before you start:** Petrol is highly flammable. Work in a well-ventilated space away from open flames, sparks, and hot surfaces. Keep a dry-powder fire extinguisher nearby. Do not smoke. Allow the engine to cool for at least 30 minutes before starting work — the exhaust pipe and engine cases hold heat long after the engine stops. 🎬 Needle Clip Position Explained "Carburetor Needle Clip Position" by Bikes and Beards — [↗ YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qP7omWBEgUg) 🎬 Needle Height on a Real Scooter Carb Practical scooter carburetor needle walkthrough — [↗ YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXxxJrA5hNY) ## How the Needle and Circlip Work A slide carburetor uses a cylindrical **throttle slide** that rises and falls as you twist the throttle. A tapered metal **needle** hangs down through the centre of the slide and sits inside the **needle jet** — a small brass tube in the carburetor body. As the slide rises, the needle also rises, and its taper progressively opens the gap between the needle and the jet, allowing more fuel to flow. The needle has a series of **grooves** machined into it near the top — usually 3, 4, or 5 grooves. A small spring clip (the **circlip**) sits in one of these grooves and rests on the top of the slide, holding the needle at a fixed height. Moving the circlip changes which groove it sits in, which raises or lowers the needle inside the jet: Throttle Slide ◀ Circlip (groove 3 — default) Groove 1 → lean Groove 2 Groove 3 (std) Groove 4 Groove 5 → rich Needle Jet CLIP UP (lower groove #) \= Needle LOWERS \= LEANER mix CLIP DOWN (higher groove #) \= Needle RISES \= RICHER mix Schematic — clip up = needle down = leaner; clip down = needle up = richer [![Real carburetor needle and circlip on a scooter — YouTube video thumbnail](https://img.youtube.com/vi/KXxxJrA5hNY/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXxxJrA5hNY) Real-world view: needle, grooves, and circlip on an actual scooter carburetor. [↗ Watch the full walkthrough on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXxxJrA5hNY) � **Counterintuitive but important:** Moving the circlip _up_ on the needle makes the mixture _leaner_, and moving it _down_ makes it _richer_. This is because moving the clip up pushes the needle body downward inside the jet, reducing fuel flow. Take a moment to picture this before you start. ## Clip Position Quick Reference
Clip PositionNeedle PositionMixture EffectWhen to Use

Groove 2Needle lowSlightly leanMild rich symptoms, warm climate
Groove 3 (middle)Needle centredStandard / stockDefault — start here
Groove 4Needle highSlightly richMild lean symptoms, cold climate
Groove 5 (bottom)Needle highestRichestCold start problems or oversized air filter

## Step-by-Step Instructions ### Step 1 — Safety Preparation Before touching anything, make sure the engine is safe to work on. 1. Turn the fuel tap (petcock) to the **OFF** position. On GY6 scooters this is typically under the seat or near the frame rail. On Piaggio models it is usually below the left panel. 2. Allow the engine to cool for at least **30 minutes** — touch the cylinder head; it should feel no warmer than room temperature. 3. Place the scooter on its centre stand on firm, level ground. 4. Lay a clean cloth or tray under the carburetor to catch any petrol residue. � **Note your starting position:** Before making any change, note which groove the circlip is in. If the adjustment makes things worse, you can always return to where you started. ### Step 2 — Access the Carburetor The carburetor is usually accessed by removing a side panel or the seat. The exact location varies by model. 1. **GY6 scooters:** Remove the left or right body panel (usually 2–4 Phillips screws). The carburetor sits on the right side of the engine, between the air filter box and the engine intake manifold. 2. **Piaggio Zip / Vespa models:** Open the underseat storage. The carburetor and air filter assembly are accessible from the right side of the frame after removing the plastic side cowl (3–5 screws). 3. Once the carburetor is visible, identify the **top cap** — the round or rectangular cover on top of the carb body. This is where the throttle cable enters. � **Take a photo first:** Before disassembling anything, photograph the carburetor, the throttle cable routing, and the throttle slide orientation. Referring to your own photos during reassembly is much easier than trying to remember. ### Step 3 — Remove the Carburetor Top Cap The top cap holds the throttle slide inside the carburetor body. Removing it gives you access to the slide and needle. 1. Locate the two to four screws around the top cap perimeter and remove them. On GY6 carbs (PD-type, CVK-type) these are Phillips screws. On Dellorto PHBG (Piaggio Zip 2T) there is a single large cap screw or a lock-ring. 2. Gently lift the top cap upward. The throttle cable and slide will come with it — **do not pull hard**. If the slide feels stuck, wiggle it gently; it may be a vacuum-type slide (CV carburetor) seated by engine vacuum. 3. Lift the slide out of the carburetor bore and let it hang from the throttle cable. Do not disconnect the cable unless necessary. 🎬 Removing the Slide & Needle — GY6 CV Carburetor "GY6 Carburetor Teardown and Needle Clip Adjustment" by ScooterDynasty — [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DcSSMw9hGLI) ### Step 4 — Remove the Needle from the Slide The needle passes through a hole in the centre of the throttle slide and is held in place by the circlip sitting in a groove. 1. Hold the slide in one hand over your tray. Look through the centre hole — you will see the top of the needle protruding slightly, with the circlip sitting in one of the grooves. 2. Using your pick or a small flat-head screwdriver, carefully lever the circlip out of its groove. Work slowly — the clip is under slight spring tension and can ping away. 3. Once the circlip is free, slide the needle downward and out through the bottom of the slide. Set the needle and circlip aside on your cloth — do not place them near an edge. 4. Count the grooves on the needle and note which groove the circlip was sitting in (1 = top groove, highest number = bottom groove). ️ **Inspect the needle while you have it out:** Run your fingernail along the needle's surface. It should be smooth with no scoring, flat spots, or visible taper wear. A worn needle will cause an inconsistent mixture no matter what groove the clip is in — replace it if in doubt (cost: €3–8). ### Step 5 — Reposition the Circlip This is the actual adjustment. Move the circlip by one groove at a time and test before moving further. 1. Decide which direction to move the clip based on your symptoms. Refer to the [Carburetor Needle Height Diagnostics guide](/diagnostics/carburetor-needle-height-diagnostics.html) if you are unsure of your symptoms. 2. **Rich mixture (black smoke, poor top speed, strong fuel smell):** Move the clip one groove _up_ toward the top of the needle (lower groove number). This lowers the needle and leans the mixture. 3. **Lean mixture (hesitation, surging, overheating):** Move the clip one groove _down_ toward the bottom of the needle (higher groove number). This raises the needle and richens the mixture. 4. To move the clip: use needle-nose pliers to grip the clip, then compress it slightly and push it into the new groove. The clip should snap in with a small click and feel secure — it should not spin freely. � **One groove at a time:** The difference between one groove and the next is significant. Always make a single-groove change, reassemble, road-test, and then decide if a further adjustment is needed. Jumping two grooves at once makes it harder to identify the correct setting. ### Step 6 — Reinstall the Needle and Slide 1. Insert the needle back up through the centre hole of the slide, pointed (tapered) end first, so the circlip end protrudes from the top. 2. The needle may have a small key or flat side that must align with a corresponding slot in the slide — check your photo from Step 2. Rotate the needle until it drops fully into position. 3. Confirm the circlip is fully seated in its groove and the needle cannot move up or down by hand. 4. Slide the throttle slide back into the carburetor body. Make sure the slide's anti-rotation pin (a small peg on the slide's side) lines up with the corresponding slot in the carburetor bore — the slide will not fit if rotated incorrectly. 5. Refit the top cap and tighten the screws evenly — do not over-tighten. ### Step 7 — Road Test and Fine-Tune 1. Turn the fuel tap back to the **ON** position. 2. Start the engine and let it warm up for 2–3 minutes without riding. 3. Take the scooter for a test ride on a quiet road. Focus on how it pulls from 25%–75% throttle — this is the mid-range where the needle has the most effect. 4. If the symptom has improved but is not fully resolved, repeat the adjustment (Steps 3–6) moving the clip by one more groove in the same direction. 5. Once mid-range feels crisp and responsive, the needle is correctly set. If idle or full-throttle behaviour is still off, those are adjusted separately with the idle screw and main jet respectively — see the related guides below. ## Troubleshooting

## Seasonal Storage Checklist If the scooter will be stored for more than 4 weeks (over winter or during extended non-use), take these steps to avoid fuel system and battery problems: 1. Remove the battery and store it indoors on a trickle charger (battery tender) — cold temperatures combined with self-discharge kill sealed lead-acid batteries. 4. � **Never run a GY6 scooter without an air filter fitted**, even briefly for testing. Without filtration, abrasive particles enter the cylinder and cause rapid bore wear within minutes of running. If the filter is being washed and is still drying, wait — do not start the engine. ## Symptoms of a Clogged Air Filter - **Loss of power and acceleration** — engine is starved of air, mixture is too rich - **Increased fuel consumption** — rich mixture burns more fuel for the same output - **Black, sooty spark plug** — carbon deposits from incomplete combustion - **Difficulty starting**, especially when warm - **Black smoke from the exhaust** - **Rough idle** that cannot be cured by carburetor adjustment alone ## Tools & Materials Required - Phillips screwdriver or 8 mm socket (airbox cover screws) - Mild dish soap and warm water (foam filters) - Clean dry cloth or paper towels - Foam filter oil (available at motorcycle shops — do not substitute with engine oil) - Replacement filter element (foam or paper, model-specific) 🎬 Video Guide — GY6 Air Filter Maintenance: Clean or Replace **Video:** "GY6 Air Filter Maintenance — Clean or Replace" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dklHU1KW2bQ) ## Procedure — GY6 Foam Filter (Most Common) 1. **Locate the airbox.** On GY6 scooters it is on the right side of the scooter under a body panel, connected to the carburetor inlet via a rubber intake boot. On most models two screws or a single wing nut secure the airbox cover. 2. **Remove the airbox cover** and lift out the foam element. Note the orientation — some elements are directional. 3. **Inspect the element.** If it is torn, deformed, or the foam has begun to crumble, replace it — cleaning a damaged filter is pointless. Also inspect the inside of the airbox housing for water, dirt, or insects and wipe it clean. 4. **Wash the foam element** in a basin of warm water with a few drops of dish soap. Squeeze gently (do not wring or twist) and work the soap through the foam until the rinse water runs completely clear. 5. **Rinse thoroughly** with clean water until all soap is gone. Soap residue left in the filter reduces airflow. 6. **Dry completely.** Squeeze out excess water gently. Pat dry with a clean cloth and leave to air-dry for at least 30–60 minutes. _The filter must be fully dry before re-oiling or reinstalling._ 7. **Apply foam filter oil.** Drizzle a small amount of filter oil onto the foam and work it in evenly with your fingers. The element should be lightly, evenly coated — not dripping wet. Excess oil gets drawn into the engine and fouls the spark plug. 8. **Reinstall the element** in the correct orientation. Refit the airbox cover and tighten the screws or wing nut firmly — air leaks around the filter housing bypass the filter entirely. 9. **Check the intake boot** (the rubber tube connecting the airbox to the carburetor) for cracks or loose clamps. A cracked boot allows unfiltered air to bypass the filter. � **No filter oil?** In an emergency, a very thin smear of clean engine oil can be used on the foam, but proper foam filter oil has a tackier consistency that traps fine dust particles more effectively. Buy dedicated filter oil for the next service. ## Procedure — Vespa / Paper Filter 1. **Access the airbox** — on Vespa Primavera and Sprint models the airbox is under the left body panel. Remove the 2–3 screws securing the panel, then open the airbox cover. 2. **Remove the paper element** and hold it up to a light source. If you cannot see light clearly through the filter paper, it must be replaced — paper filters cannot be washed back to full effectiveness. 3. **Tap the element gently** against your palm to dislodge loose dust, if the element is only lightly soiled. Do not use compressed air — high pressure damages the paper fibres. 4. **Wipe out the airbox housing** with a dry cloth. 5. **Fit the new or cleaned element** and reclose the airbox. Ensure the cover seal is seated correctly — even a small gap allows unfiltered air in. ## Service Intervals

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; A big bore kit is the most impactful single upgrade you can make to a GY6 engine. By fitting a larger cylinder and matched piston, displacement increases — bringing noticeably improved acceleration and higher top speed without requiring exotic parts. This guide covers what big bore kits are, how to choose the right one, and how to install it correctly. ## What Is a Big Bore Kit? A big bore kit replaces the stock cylinder, piston, piston rings, and sometimes the cylinder head with larger-bore equivalents. The crankcase, crankshaft, and valve train typically remain stock. The displacement increase comes entirely from the wider bore — stroke length stays the same. On a standard GY6 150cc engine (`157QMJ`, 57 mm bore), a 171cc upgrade uses a 61 mm bore cylinder. This 4 mm bore increase raises displacement from 150 cc to approximately 171 cc — a gain of about 14 percent. ## Available Upgrades for GY6 Engines
EngineStock BoreBig Bore OptionNew DisplacementMachining Required?
GY6 50cc (139QMB)39 mm47 mm kit (70cc)~70 ccNo — drop-in on most B-Block cases
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)57 mm61 mm kit (171cc)~171 ccNo — fits stock A-Block cases
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)57 mm63 mm kit (180cc)~180 ccYes — case boring required
**⚠️ Beware of "No Machining Required" 63 mm Kits:** Some vendors sell 63 mm kits claiming no case machining is needed. Experienced builders strongly advise against these — the cylinder wall is too thin for long-term reliability at that bore size without proper case preparation. If you want 180cc, have the cases professionally bored. ## What to Buy — Kit Components A reputable big bore kit should include: a new cylinder (barrel), piston with circlips, piston rings, a base gasket, and a head gasket. Some kits include a matching cylinder head; others require you to reuse or source a head separately. Quality varies enormously. Key markers of a good kit: - Cylinder bore is honed (cross-hatch pattern visible inside) — not just drilled - Piston rings fit the ring grooves precisely — no side-play when pushed down - Ring end-gaps are within specification — check with feeler gauges (see below) - Base gasket is the correct thickness for your head gasket combination ## Tools Required - Socket set and combination spanners (8, 10, 12, 14, 17 mm) - Torque wrench (capable of 10–50 Nm) - Feeler gauges - Piston ring compressor (or careful hands) - Gasket scraper / razor blade - Engine oil and assembly lube - Thread-locking compound (Loctite 243 or equivalent) - Camera or phone — photograph everything before disassembly ## Installation Procedure ### Step 1: Prepare the Engine 1. Allow the engine to cool completely. Drain the engine oil. 2. Remove the seat, bodywork panels, and air filter assembly to gain access to the engine. 3. Disconnect the spark plug cap. Remove the spark plug. 4. For easier access, consider removing the engine from the frame (disconnect the carburetor, exhaust, wiring loom, rear shock mount, and engine hanger bolt). ### Step 2: Remove the Cylinder Head and Cylinder 1. Remove the valve cover (cam cap). Photograph the cam chain routing before disassembly. 2. Rotate the engine to Top Dead Centre (TDC) on the compression stroke — both valves closed, timing mark aligned. 3. Remove the cam chain tensioner bolt and slide the tensioner out. 4. Undo the camshaft bearing cap (two bolts). Lift out the camshaft carefully, keeping the cam chain loop over the sprocket — secure it with a zip tie through the chain to prevent it dropping into the case. 5. Undo the four cylinder head nuts in a cross pattern. Lift the head off — it may need gentle tapping with a rubber mallet. Do not use a metal hammer directly on the head. 6. Lift the cylinder off the studs. The piston will be exposed. Place a clean rag over the crankcase mouth immediately to prevent debris entering. ### Step 3: Remove the Old Piston 1. Note which way the piston arrow or notch faces (it must point toward the exhaust side on reassembly). 2. Use a small screwdriver or circlip pliers to remove the piston pin circlips from both sides of the piston. Keep these — they are reusable if undamaged. 3. Push the piston pin out by hand or with a dowel. The piston will slide off the connecting rod. ### Step 4: Check and Prepare the New Components 1. Inspect the new cylinder bore — it should be smooth with a visible cross-hatch honing pattern. 2. Check piston ring end-gaps by placing each ring individually inside the new cylinder bore and measuring the gap with feeler gauges. Standard acceptable range: 0.15–0.40 mm. Replace rings if gaps are outside this range. 3. Lubricate the cylinder bore, piston, and piston pin with fresh engine oil. 4. Install the piston rings onto the new piston — top ring, second ring, then oil scraper ring. Stagger the ring gaps 120° apart around the piston to minimise blow-by. ### Step 5: Install the New Piston and Cylinder 1. Fit the new piston onto the connecting rod with the arrow or "EX" marking facing the exhaust port. Insert the piston pin and reinstall the circlips — ensure both circlips are fully seated in their grooves. 2. Clean the crankcase mating surface and cylinder base — remove all old gasket material. 3. Place the new base gasket on the crankcase studs (dry — no sealant). 4. Oil the cylinder bore again. Compress the piston rings using a ring compressor or your thumbs. Carefully lower the new cylinder over the piston, keeping the cam chain guided through the chain tunnel. 5. Seat the cylinder fully on the base gasket. ### Step 6: Reassemble the Top End 1. Install the new head gasket. Lower the cylinder head into place over the studs. 2. Fit the head nuts finger-tight, then torque in a cross pattern: 10–12 Nm for M6 studs. Do not overtighten — the aluminium will strip. 3. Reinstall the camshaft, aligning the timing marks on the cam sprocket with the marks on the cylinder head. 4. Reinstall the cam chain tensioner. Reinstall the valve cover. 5. Reinstall the spark plug: 10–14 Nm. ### Step 7: Re-jet the Carburetor A larger engine displaces more air per intake stroke. The stock main jet (typically 95–105 for a 150cc GY6) will run lean with a 171cc cylinder. Fit a larger main jet — start 5–10 sizes up from stock (e.g., jet #108 for a 61 mm / 171cc build). Test and adjust until the spark plug reads a light tan colour after a full-throttle run. **💡 Re-torque After First Heat Cycle:** After the engine has warmed up to operating temperature for the first time and cooled back down, re-torque the cylinder head nuts. Aluminium expands and contracts significantly with temperature, which can cause head gasket settling. This step prevents head gasket failure in the first few hundred kilometres. ## Common Mistakes - **Forgetting to re-jet:** Running lean after a displacement increase will burn the piston. Always re-jet. - **Installing rings with gaps aligned:** Piston rings must have staggered gaps. Aligned gaps cause excessive blow-by and oil consumption. - **Overtorquing the head:** The aluminium head strips very easily. Use a torque wrench — don't rely on feel. - **Dropping the cam chain:** Secure it with a zip tie before removing the camshaft. Retrieving a dropped cam chain can mean splitting the cases. - **Skipping the break-in period:** For the first 200–300 km after a big bore install, avoid full throttle. Vary engine speed to allow the rings to bed in properly. ## Expected Performance Gains A 150cc → 171cc big bore conversion on a GY6 scooter typically delivers: 10–15% more torque at low-to-mid RPM, noticeably stronger acceleration from a standstill, and a modest top speed increase (2–5 km/h in most cases). The biggest benefit is felt in the mid-range — the scooter pulls harder up hills and when two-up riding. For further gains, the big bore upgrade pairs well with a performance exhaust, upgraded variator rollers matched to the new power delivery, and — if running carburetion — a matching performance air filter and jet kit.

DOT 5 (silicone-based) is **completely incompatible** with DOT 3/4/5.1 systems and must never be used unless the entire system has been flushed and rebuilt. ## Tools & Materials Required - 8 mm ring spanner (bleed nipple) - Phillips screwdriver (master cylinder reservoir cap screws) - Fresh, sealed DOT 4 brake fluid (100–200 ml is sufficient for one circuit) - Clear vinyl bleed tube (~30 cm, 4–5 mm inner diameter) - Small glass jar or container for old fluid - Syringe or turkey baster (for reservoir management) - Rags and newspaper to protect painted surfaces - Nitrile gloves 🎬 Video Guide — Bleeding the Front Brake on a 150cc GY6 Scooter **Video:** "Bleeding the Front Brake on a 150cc GY6 Scooter" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nhfPUISx-FU) ## Step-by-Step Brake Bleed Procedure ### Preparation 1. **Protect surrounding surfaces** — lay rags over the scooter's painted panels, plastics, and the fuel tank around the handlebar area. Brake fluid contact causes immediate paint damage. 2. **Locate the brake caliper bleed nipple** — a small valve on the caliper body with a rubber dust cap. Remove the dust cap. 3. **Attach the bleed tube** over the nipple. Place the other end into the collection jar. Loop the tube upward above the caliper height — this prevents air from being drawn back into the system between pumps. ### Draining & Filling 4. **Open the master cylinder reservoir** on the handlebar — remove the two Phillips screws, lift off the cap, and remove the rubber diaphragm. Keep the reservoir level at all times to prevent air entry. 5. **Note the fluid color** — fresh DOT 4 is clear/pale yellow. Old fluid is amber to dark brown. Heavily contaminated fluid may be almost black. 6. **Top up the reservoir** with fresh fluid to the MAX line before opening the bleed nipple. This prevents the reservoir from running dry and drawing air into the system. ### Bleeding (Two-Person or One-Person Method) 7. **Open the bleed nipple** ½ turn counter-clockwise. Old fluid will begin to flow by gravity. 8. **Pump-bleed cycle** — squeeze the brake lever _slowly_ to the handlebar. With the lever held in, open the nipple ½ turn and allow fluid to flow out. Close the nipple before releasing the lever. Repeat this cycle 8–10 times. This pushes old fluid out faster and purges air bubbles. 9. **Watch the reservoir constantly** — top up with fresh fluid every 3–4 pump cycles. If the reservoir runs empty, air enters the system and you must start over. 10. **Continue until** the fluid flowing out of the bleed tube is clear and pale yellow (matching the fresh fluid in the bottle), with no air bubbles visible in the tube. 11. **Final close:** with the brake lever squeezed to the handlebar, close the bleed nipple firmly (5–8 Nm — snug, not over-tight). Release the lever. ### Finishing 12. **Top up the reservoir** to the MAX line with fresh fluid. Refit the rubber diaphragm (ensure it seats without folds) and reinstall the cap and screws. 13. **Pump the lever** several times — it should feel firm throughout its travel with no sponginess. If still spongy, air remains in the system and the bleed procedure must be repeated. 14. **Refit the bleed nipple dust cap.** 15. **Wipe down all surfaces** that may have been contaminated with fluid. Check carefully around the reservoir cap and bleed nipple. 16. **Test ride carefully** at low speed before normal use. � **One-person bleeding tip:** A cheap vacuum bleeder kit (syringe + tube with one-way valve, ~€10 online) makes solo bleeding much easier and faster. You can also use the gravity-bleed method — open the nipple ½ turn and let fluid drip out by gravity while keeping the reservoir topped up, no lever pumping needed. Gravity bleed is slower but foolproof for removing old fluid. ## Service Intervals

Check the reservoir level before you start and remove a small amount with a syringe if it is at MAX — otherwise it will overflow when the piston is retracted. 1. **Support the scooter** on its centre stand on a flat, stable surface. 2. **Remove the two caliper mounting bolts** (usually 10 mm) and slide the caliper off the rotor. Support the caliper with a wire or bungee cord — do not let it hang by the brake line. 3. **Remove the pad retaining pin** (a bolt or cotter pin depending on caliper type) and slide the old pads out of the caliper. 4. **Inspect the brake rotor** for deep grooves, scoring, or cracks. Minimum thickness is typically stamped on the rotor. A heavily grooved rotor reduces new pad effectiveness and should be replaced. 5. **Retract the caliper piston:** place the old pad against the piston face and press it back into the caliper body using a large flat-head screwdriver or C-clamp. Push slowly and evenly. The piston must be fully retracted to accommodate the thickness of new pads. 6. **Clean the caliper carrier** with brake cleaner — remove all dust, rust, and debris from the pad slide channels. 7. **Apply a thin film of copper grease** to the back face of each new pad and to the caliper slide pins. Do not get any grease on the friction surface or the rotor. 8. **Insert the new pads** into the caliper and refit the retaining pin. Reinstall the caliper and torque the mounting bolts to **25–30 Nm**. 9. **Pump the brake lever** 10–15 times until the lever feels firm — this pushes the pistons out to contact the new pads. Check the brake fluid reservoir level and top up to MAX if needed. 10. **Bed in the pads:** perform 5–6 firm stops from 30 km/h before normal riding. This transfers a thin even layer of pad material onto the rotor surface for optimal friction. ## Part B — Rear Drum Brake Shoe Replacement (GY6) 1. **Remove the rear wheel:** loosen the axle nut, disconnect the rear brake cable or rod, and slide the wheel off. Place the scooter on a paddock stand or support it securely. 2. **Expose the brake shoes:** the drum is integral to the wheel hub. The shoes are mounted on a brake plate (backing plate) attached to the swingarm. With the wheel removed, the shoes are visible. 3. **Photograph the spring arrangement** before removing anything — reassembly requires knowing exactly where each return spring attaches. 4. **Remove the return springs** using brake spring pliers or needle-nose pliers. Slide the old shoes off the pivot pins and cam. 5. **Inspect the drum surface** (inside the wheel hub) for scoring. Light scores are normal; deep grooves require drum skimming or replacement. 6. **Clean the backing plate** with brake cleaner. Apply a small amount of high-temperature grease to the shoe contact points on the backing plate — the raised pads where the shoe metal slides. Do not apply any grease near the friction surface. 7. **Fit the new shoes** onto the pivot pins and cam. Reattach the return springs — the springs should pull the shoes back toward each other (away from the drum). 8. **Reinstall the wheel** and tighten the axle nut to the specified torque (typically 50–60 Nm). 9. **Adjust the brake cable or rod** so the rear brake has approximately 10–15 mm of free play at the lever/pedal tip before resistance begins. Too little free play causes the brake to drag; too much increases stopping distance. 10. **Test** by walking the scooter and applying the rear brake firmly several times before riding. ## GY6 Brake Pad & Shoe Reference

### Understanding the Adjusters Two screws control most of the tune: - **Idle speed screw (throttle stop screw):** Controls minimum throttle position — turning it clockwise raises idle RPM, counter-clockwise lowers it. - **Air/fuel mixture screw (pilot screw):** Controls the fuel richness at idle and low throttle. Located under a small brass plug on the carburetor body (sometimes covered by an anti-tamper cap). Turning counter-clockwise (out) richens the mixture; clockwise (in) leans it out. ### Step-by-Step Procedure 1 Initial Mixture Screw Setting 1. Gently turn the mixture screw clockwise until it seats lightly. **Do not force it** — the needle tip is fragile. 2. Back it out the following number of turns as a starting baseline:
EngineStarting Position

2 Set Idle Speed 1. Start the engine and allow it to reach full operating temperature (10 minutes minimum). 2. Using the idle speed screw, adjust RPM to the target range (see specifications table above). 3. If you do not have a tachometer, set idle to the lowest stable speed at which the engine will not stall. 3 Fine-Tune the Air/Fuel Mixture 1. With the engine at full operating temperature and idle set, slowly turn the mixture screw counter-clockwise (richer) in ¼-turn increments. Pause 10–15 seconds after each adjustment. 2. Listen: RPM should rise as you approach the ideal mixture. Note the position where RPM peaks. 3. From the peak-RPM position, turn the screw clockwise (leaner) by ¼ turn. This is your optimal idle mixture setting. 4. Re-adjust the idle speed screw to bring the RPM back to the target range. 5. Snap the throttle open quickly and release — the engine should rev cleanly without hesitation or stumble. If it stumbles, richen the mixture slightly (counter-clockwise ¼ turn). 4 Float Level Adjustment An incorrectly set float is one of the most common causes of GY6 carburetor problems: too high causes rich running, fuel overflow, and stalling at idle; too low causes lean surge and bog. 🎬 Float Adjustment Technique **Video:** "How to Adjust a Float on a Carburetor | Simple Trick!" — Demonstrates the proper technique for bending the float tab without damaging it. 1. Remove the float bowl (bottom of carburetor, held by one screw). Drain any fuel into a rag. 2. Hold the carburetor body with the float upright (as if gravity were pulling it closed). 3. The bottom of the float should be parallel to the carburetor body gasket surface. Typical specification: **14–16 mm** from the gasket surface to the bottom of the float. 4. To adjust, gently bend the small metal tab that contacts the needle valve until the float sits at the correct height. 5. Reinstall float bowl with a new gasket if available. Tighten the bowl screw snugly — do not overtighten (it is often plastic-threaded). � **Tip:** If the float bowl gasket leaks, a thin smear of petrol-resistant RTV sealant works as a temporary fix, but a proper replacement O-ring or gasket is always better. 5 Pilot Jet & Main Jet (Cleaning) Before adjusting, confirm the jets are clean. A partially blocked pilot jet causes lean stumble at idle; a blocked main jet causes flat top-speed. 1. Remove the pilot jet (see specifications table for sizes) and main jet. 2. Spray carburetor cleaner through the jet holes and blow clear with compressed air. **Never use wire** — it enlarges the orifice. 3. Hold the jet up to light — you should see a clean round hole straight through. 4. Reinstall jets snug but do not overtighten (they strip easily). ### Symptom Diagnosis Quick Reference

This guide covers a thorough disassembly-and-clean — going further than a quick spray of carb cleaner — for the standard slide-type carburetors (PD18J / PD22J / PD24J / CVK) fitted to GY6 139QMB (50cc) and 157QMJ (125cc / 150cc) engines. ## Video Walkthrough ## Tools & Materials - JIS cross-head screwdrivers (sizes #1 and #2) — not standard Phillips - Flat-blade screwdriver, 3 mm and 5 mm - Aerosol carburetor cleaner (non-residue formula) - Compressed air with fine nozzle - Small wire brush (soft brass bristles) - Clean rag or lint-free cloth - Parts tray or egg carton (to sort jets and screws) - New float-bowl gasket (O-ring or flat, depending on carb model) - Nitrile gloves and eye protection Fire hazard: Work in a well-ventilated area away from ignition sources. Petrol and carburetor cleaner are highly flammable. Disconnect the fuel tap (petcock) before removing the float bowl. ## Step-by-Step Procedure ### 1 — Preparation 1. Allow the engine to cool completely. A warm carburetor is easier to smell fumes from, but a hot engine is a burn hazard. 2. Turn the fuel tap to the **OFF** or **PRI** (prime) position so no fuel flows to the carburetor. 3. Remove the side panel or access cover on your scooter to expose the carburetor body. 4. Place a rag or drain pan under the float bowl to catch residual fuel. ### 2 — Remove the Carburetor 1. Loosen the intake manifold clamp screw (the band clamp connecting carburetor to engine inlet). Do not remove — just loosen until the carburetor can twist free. 2. Loosen the air-box clamp in the same way on the air-filter side. 3. Disconnect the throttle cable: compress the cable end and unhook it from the slide. Note the cable routing. 4. Detach the fuel line from the carburetor inlet nipple. Plug or clamp the line to prevent dripping. 5. Disconnect the choke cable (or automatic choke wiring connector if fitted). 6. Twist and pull the carburetor free from both clamps. Set it on your work surface. ### 3 — Disassemble the Float Bowl 1. Unscrew the float-bowl drain screw (bottom of bowl, if present) and drain remaining fuel into a container. 2. Remove the float-bowl retaining screw(s) — usually one or two at the bottom or side. Lift the bowl away. 3. Inspect the bowl for sediment, rust particles, or a dark varnish residue. These indicate stale fuel contamination. 4. Remove the float by pushing out its hinge pin sideways. The float and needle will come away as one unit. 5. Unscrew the main jet (brass screw in the centre of the carb body) using a flat-blade screwdriver. Note its size — it is stamped on the side (e.g., `#75`, `#85`, `#98`). 6. Unscrew the pilot jet (smaller brass screw nearby, sometimes recessed). Note its size as well. | Engine | Typical Main Jet | Pilot Jet | Carburetor | |---|---|---|---| | GY6 50cc (139QMB) | #75–#78 | #35–#38 | PD18J | | GY6 125cc (152QMI) | #95–#98 | #38–#42 | PD22J / CVK22 | | GY6 150cc (157QMJ) | #98–#105 | #38–#42 | PD24J / CVK24 | ### 4 — Clean All Components 1. **Float bowl:** Spray interior with carburetor cleaner, scrub with a soft brush, rinse, dry with compressed air. 2. **Main jet:** Hold up to light and check that the hole is clear and round. Spray cleaner through it. If blocked, use a bristle from the wire brush — never a drill bit or wire, which will enlarge the calibrated orifice. 3. **Pilot jet:** Same process. The pilot jet feeds fuel at idle and low throttle; a partially blocked pilot jet causes rough idle and stumbling below ¼ throttle. 4. **Carburetor body passages:** Spray cleaner into every port and passage you can see, including the emulsion tube holes (the small holes in the main bore). Follow with compressed air from the opposite side to clear debris outward. 5. **Needle and slide:** Remove the top cap of the carburetor to extract the slide. Inspect the needle for wear (grooves, bends). Clean the slide bore with a cloth dampened in cleaner. 6. **Air/fuel mixture screw:** Count and record how many turns out it is currently set before removing. Remove it carefully (it may have a small O-ring, washer, and spring). Clean the passage with cleaner and air. Reinstall to the recorded position. Tip: If the carburetor body shows brown or black varnish inside the float bowl or emulsion passages, soak it for 30 minutes in a commercial carburetor dip (or a solution of acetone and water). This dissolves hardened gum deposits that aerosol cleaner cannot shift. ### 5 — Inspect the Float & Needle Valve 1. Shake the float gently next to your ear — if you hear liquid sloshing inside, the float has a pinhole and must be replaced. A sinking float will cause fuel to flood the engine. 2. Inspect the tip of the needle valve (the rubber or brass cone that seats against the float seat). If it shows wear or has a groove, replace it — a worn needle valve will cause fuel overflow and a rich condition. 3. Set float height: with the float bowl mating face horizontal, the float arms should be roughly parallel to that face. Bend the small tab that contacts the needle valve to adjust if needed. Refer to your engine's service manual for the exact specification (typically 14–16 mm on GY6 157QMJ). ### 6 — Reassembly 1. Install jets finger-tight, then snug (do not overtighten — they are brass in an aluminium body). 2. Refit the float and hinge pin. 3. Install a new float-bowl O-ring or gasket if the old one is compressed or cracked. 4. Refit the float bowl and tighten evenly. 5. Reinstall the slide and needle (ensure the needle clip is seated in the correct groove — middle groove for standard tune). 6. Refit the carburetor to the scooter, reversing the removal steps. Ensure both clamps are properly tightened to prevent air leaks. 7. Reconnect fuel line, throttle cable, and choke cable. 8. Turn the fuel tap on and check for leaks before starting. ### 7 — First-Start Tuning 1. Start the engine and allow it to reach operating temperature (approximately 5 minutes of running). 2. Adjust the idle speed screw (the large thumb or flat-blade screw on the side of the carb body) until idle is stable at approximately 1,500–1,800 rpm. 3. Adjust the air/fuel mixture screw (the small recessed screw) ½ turn at a time, waiting 30 seconds between adjustments, until idle is smooth and highest. Typical range is 1½ to 2½ turns out from gently seated. 4. Snap the throttle open and release it — the engine should rev cleanly without hesitation or hanging. If you have added an aftermarket exhaust, performance air filter, or high-compression piston, rejetting is essential. ## Understanding the Throttle Zones The GY6 slide-type carburetor (PD-series or CVK) controls the mixture across the throttle range via different circuits. Knowing which circuit governs each zone tells you which component to adjust: - **0–¼ throttle (idle and off-idle):** Governed by the pilot jet and the air/fuel mixture screw. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Added: 2026-05-11  |  Sources: [buggydepot.com](https://www.buggydepot.com/tech-center/gy6-150cc-ignition-troubleshooting-guide-no-spark/), [moowiring.com](https://moowiring.com/2025/05/24/gy6-dc-cdi-wiring-diagram/) GY6 Ignition CDI Carburettor Fuel Injection A GY6-engine scooter that cranks normally but produces no spark is one of the most common breakdown scenarios. The ignition system has three main electrical components that work together to fire the spark plug: the **stator / pick-up coil**, the **CDI unit** (Capacitor Discharge Ignition), and the **ignition coil**. This guide walks through a logical, test-before-replace diagnostic sequence so you replace only the component that has actually failed. **Applies to:** All GY6 50 cc (139QMB) and 125/150 cc (157QMJ / QMI152) engines — both carburetor and fuel-injected variants. The AC-CDI ignition circuit is identical across carburetted and EFI models. ⚠️ **Safety:** Work with the ignition off and the kill switch in the OFF position except when explicitly told to crank the engine during a test step. Keep hands and tools clear of the flywheel and cooling fan during cranking. ## Understanding the GY6 Ignition Circuit On all standard GY6 engines the CDI is an AC-CDI: the stator generates its own alternating current to power the CDI capacitor — the main battery is not involved in spark production. Current flow is: stator charging coil → CDI capacitor → CDI trigger from pick-up coil → ignition coil primary winding → secondary winding → HT lead → spark plug. The most commonly sold replacement CDIs for GY6 scooters are the 5-pin AC-CDI (most 50 cc models) and the 6-pin AC-CDI (most 125/150 cc models). DC-CDI units (powered from the battery) are found on some fuel-injected variants and EFI conversion kits. ## Tools Required - Digital multimeter (AC and DC voltage, resistance) - Inline spark tester or spare known-good spark plug - Screwdrivers (Phillips and flat) - Side cutters and electrical tape or crimp connectors for any wiring repairs ## Step 1 — Confirm the Symptom Is No Spark 1. Remove the spark plug and reconnect the HT lead to it. 2. Lay the plug body against the engine casing (good earth contact is essential). 3. Ask a helper to crank the engine for 3–4 seconds while you watch the plug gap. 4. A healthy spark is bright blue-white and consistent. A weak orange/yellow spark or no spark at all requires investigation. ## Step 2 — Inspect the Basics Before Testing Components Before reaching for the multimeter, visually inspect these quick-fail points — they account for roughly 40 % of no-spark faults: - **Spark plug condition:** A fouled, cracked, or incorrectly gapped plug will not spark. Replace it with a new `NGK C7HSA` (50 cc) or `NGK CR7HSA` (125/150 cc) and retest. - **Kill switch:** Disconnect the kill-switch wire from the CDI. Many kill switches fail internally and earth the CDI permanently. Retest with it disconnected. - **Side-stand switch:** Some models have a side-stand interlock that grounds the CDI when the stand is down. Raise the stand and retest, or disconnect the switch wire. - **Earth/ground wires:** Inspect every earth strap on the engine, frame, and battery. A corroded or broken ground is a very common cause of no-spark. - **HT lead and cap:** A cracked lead or a loose cap will break the secondary circuit. Replace if the rubber insulation is hard or cracked. ## Step 3 — Test the Pick-Up Coil (Trigger Coil) The pick-up coil sits inside the left-hand engine cover behind the flywheel and generates the timing pulse that tells the CDI when to fire. 1. Locate the pick-up coil connector — typically a 2-pin or 3-pin connector coming out of the stator cover. On a 5-pin CDI the trigger wires are usually `white/green` and `green`; on 6-pin CDIs, `white/green` and `black/white`. 2. Set the multimeter to AC voltage. With the connector unplugged, backprobe the two trigger pins and crank the engine. 3. A healthy pick-up coil produces **0.5–2.5 V AC** at cranking speed. 4. If voltage is 0 V, set the meter to resistance (Ω). A healthy pick-up coil measures approximately **80–120 Ω** across the two trigger wires. Open-circuit (OL) or a short to earth means a failed coil. 5. Also test the stator charging coil (the yellow/yellow wires): should produce **2–5 V AC** at cranking speed and read **1–3 Ω** resistance. ## Step 4 — Test the Ignition Coil The ignition coil takes the CDI's capacitor discharge and steps it up to ~15,000–25,000 V for the spark plug. Testing it in-circuit is straightforward: 1. Disconnect the primary coil wires (normally `orange` from the CDI and `black` earth). 2. Measure resistance across the primary winding (the two thin wires): should read **0.3–1.5 Ω**. Open-circuit = failed coil. 3. Measure across the secondary winding (between the HT cap and the earth wire, with the spark plug removed from the cap): should read **6–15 kΩ**. 4. If both windings are in spec but there is still no spark, the coil may have an internal insulation breakdown only visible under the load of a real discharge. Swap with a known-good coil as the final check. ## Step 5 — Test and Replace the CDI Unit CDI units are solid-state and cannot be repaired — they must be swapped. However, test the input signals first so you know whether a new CDI will cure the fault: 1. Plug the CDI back in. Backprobe the charging input pins (yellow wires) at the CDI connector with the multimeter on AC voltage. Crank the engine. You should see **at least 2 V AC**. If you see 0 V, the fault is upstream (stator/wiring), not the CDI. 2. Backprobe the trigger input pins. Crank. You should see a pulsing voltage (0.5–2.5 V AC). If no pulse, the pick-up coil or its wiring is the fault. 3. If both inputs are present but there is still no spark at the output (ignition coil primary), the CDI has failed internally. Replace it. ## Replacing the CDI Identify the correct replacement before ordering — count the pins on your CDI connector (5-pin or 6-pin) and note whether your engine uses AC-CDI (most carburetted and EFI scooters) or DC-CDI (battery-powered, found on some EFI conversions). Unplug the harness connector (press the release tab, pull straight out). 3. Fit the new CDI, routing the harness away from hot engine parts and sharp edges. 4. Reconnect, crank, and confirm spark before reassembling bodywork. ## Diagnostic Quick-Reference

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## How the GY6 CVT Works The Continuously Variable Transmission (CVT) on GY6 scooters consists of three main assemblies: the **variator** (primary pulley on the crankshaft), the **rear clutch bell/secondary pulley** (on the transmission input shaft), and the **drive belt** that runs between them. As engine RPM rises, centrifugal rollers inside the variator push the pulley faces together, forcing the belt to ride higher — effectively changing the gear ratio automatically without any driver input. ## When to Replace
ComponentReplacement IntervalSymptoms of Wear
Drive beltEvery 8,000–12,000 km (or sooner if cracked)Slipping, loss of acceleration, jerky takeoff, visible cracks on belt edges
Variator rollersEvery 10,000–15,000 kmHesitation at mid-throttle, flat acceleration curve, rattling from CVT cover
Clutch springsEvery 15,000–20,000 kmClutch engaging too early (creep at idle), poor low-speed drivability
CVT cover gasketWhenever cover is removedOil/grease seeping from CVT cover seam
️ **Safety first:** Work on a cold engine only. The variator and clutch bell reach high temperatures during operation. Ensure the scooter is on its centre stand on a flat, stable surface. ## Tools Required - Socket set (metric): 8 mm, 10 mm, 17 mm, 22 mm (or as required for your specific nuts) - **Variator holding tool** (universal GY6 type) — essential; do not attempt to use a screwdriver to jam the variator - Impact wrench or breaker bar (the variator nut is torqued very tight) - Torque wrench - Soft mallet or rubber hammer - Cleaning rags - Replacement belt (confirm dimensions — see Specifications below) - Replacement rollers if required ## Belt Specification Reference
EngineTypical Belt SizeNotes
GY6 50cc (139QMB)669 × 18 × 30Most common on BTC Riva, La Souris, Santini 50cc
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)835 × 20 × 30 or 842 × 20 × 30Verify against your specific model
The three numbers represent: overall length × top width × angle. Always confirm the correct size with your parts supplier before ordering — some Chinese scooter variants deviate from standard sizes. 🎬 Video Guide — Simplest Way to Replace a GY6 CV Belt **Video:** "Simplest Way to Replace GY6 CV Belt" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XakWj8YM_P4) ## Step-by-Step Procedure 1 Remove the CVT Cover 1. Place the scooter on its centre stand on level ground. 2. Locate the CVT cover on the left side of the engine (the large plastic or alloy cover with ventilation slots). 3. Remove all cover bolts — typically 6–8 bolts of 8 mm or 10 mm. Keep them together; they are often different lengths. 4. Gently tap the cover with a soft mallet to break the gasket seal if it is stuck. Do not pry against the casting — it cracks easily. 5. Remove the cover. Inspect the inside for belt dust, cracked rubber fragments, or oil contamination (indicates a crankshaft seal leak). 2 Remove the Drive Belt 1. With the cover off, you will see the drive belt running between the two pulleys. 2. Compress (push together) the faces of the rear clutch pulley by hand while simultaneously lifting the belt off the front variator pulley. This creates slack in the belt loop. 3. Slide the belt off the rear clutch, then off the front variator. If the belt is stiff or cracked, it may snap during removal — wear eye protection. 4. Inspect the belt: cracks along the edge, fraying, glazing, or visible rubber chunks missing all indicate the belt needs replacement. 3 Remove the Variator (for roller replacement) 1. Use the variator holding tool to lock the front pulley against rotation. 2. With an impact wrench or breaker bar, remove the variator nut (right-hand thread — turn counter-clockwise to loosen). This nut is typically torqued to **49 Nm (36 ft-lb)**. 3. Slide off the outer face of the variator. Note the orientation — there is often an arrow or chamfer indicating the correct fitting direction. 4. Remove the rollers. There are typically 6 rollers inside a guide cage. Inspect each one: flat spots, grooves worn into the roller surface, or irregular wear all indicate replacement is needed. 5. **Roller specifications by engine:** - GY6 50cc (139QMB): **16×13 mm** @ 7.5–8.5 g (OEM stock weight varies; aftermarket range 5–11.5g) - GY6 125cc (152QMI): **18×14 mm** @ 12–13 g (OEM ~12.8g) - GY6 150cc (157QMJ): **18×14 mm** @ 12–14 g _Always use the correct diameter (16×13, 18×14, etc.) for your engine — mixing sizes causes CVT failure. Heavier rollers delay engagement (better top speed); lighter rollers engage earlier (better acceleration). Do not deviate more than 2 g from stock unless tuning for a specific purpose._ 6. Clean the variator ramp surfaces and roller guides with a rag. **Do not use grease on the rollers** — they must run dry. Grease attracts belt dust and causes premature wear. 7. Install new rollers in the guide cage, reinstall the outer variator face, and torque the nut to **49 Nm**. 4 Install the New Belt & Reassemble 1. Route the new belt over the rear clutch pulley first, ensuring it sits centrally in the groove. 2. While compressing the rear pulley faces together, loop the belt over the front variator. Release the rear pulley — the spring tension will pull the belt taut. 3. Rotate the rear wheel by hand to seat the belt evenly and check that it tracks centrally on both pulleys without twisting. 4. Clean the CVT cover interior and replace the gasket if torn or compressed flat. 5. Refit the CVT cover. Tighten bolts in a cross pattern to approximately **10–12 Nm**. Do not overtighten — the cover threads strip easily. � **Break-in tip:** After fitting a new belt, avoid full-throttle acceleration for the first 100–200 km. New belts need time to seat and conform to the pulley surfaces. Premature hard acceleration can glaze or crack a new belt prematurely. ## Torque Specifications Summary

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## What Is Intake Flooding on an EFI Scooter? **This guide covers EFI (fuel-injected) GY6 engines only** — scooters with a throttle body, fuel injector, and ECU. There is no float bowl or needle valve. If your scooter has a carburetor with a float bowl, see the [GY6 Carburetor Intake Flooding guide](gy6-hard-start-intake-flooding.html) instead. Most hard-start guides tell you the engine is starved of fuel. This guide covers the opposite problem: **too much fuel in the intake**. When excess petrol pools in the intake port or cylinder, the spark plug drowns and cannot ignite the mixture. The engine cranks normally but refuses to fire — or fires once with a cough of black smoke and immediately dies. On EFI GY6 engines, intake flooding has two common causes: a **cracked rubber intake insulator** (the mounting block between the throttle body and the cylinder head) or a **leaking fuel injector** that drips raw fuel into the intake port when the engine is switched off. Both allow liquid fuel to pool in the port rather than being delivered as a precisely metered mist on demand. ### Video: EFI Intake Flooding — Real Example Video shows a real EFI scooter with fuel pooled in the intake — cracked insulator and injector leak identified and repaired. ## Symptoms
SymptomFlooding Likelihood
Engine cranks freely but will not fire at allHigh
Starts briefly, fires once or twice, then immediately diesVery high
Black smoke from the exhaust on the rare occasions it firesVery high
Strong petrol smell from the airbox or around the engineHigh
Spark plug electrode is wet and smells of petrol when removedDefinitive confirmation
Engine starts after leaving it overnight (fuel evaporates)High

**Do not confuse with a lean no-start.** A lean no-start (blocked injector, failed fuel pump, bad TPS) produces a dry, light-coloured spark plug. An intake flood produces a wet, fuel-soaked plug. Remove the plug first — it tells you immediately which problem you are dealing with. If you have ECU fault codes, check the [EFI Fuel Injection Troubleshooting guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-fuel-injection-troubleshooting.html) first. ## The Two Main Causes ### Cause 1 — Cracked Intake Insulator (Manifold Gasket Block) The intake insulator is the rubber block connecting the throttle body to the cylinder head inlet port. It absorbs vibration and provides a heat barrier. After several years, the rubber cracks — often across the top, along the inner bore, or at the mounting flange. On an EFI engine, a cracked insulator allows unmetered air in (confusing the ECU's fuelling calculations) and, critically, lets condensed or dripped fuel bypass the intake air path and pool directly in the port. ![Cracked GY6 rubber intake insulator held in hand, showing a visible crack across the top of the inner bore](/repair-guides/images/intake_gasket_broken.jpg) **Cracked intake insulator.** Crack visible across the top of the inner bore — this is the rubber block between the throttle body and the cylinder head. Once cracked, it must be replaced; silicone is not a permanent fix. ![GY6 EFI engine intake port with fuel pooled inside, visible as wet residue around the port opening](/repair-guides/images/intake_full_of_fuel.png) **Intake port flooded with fuel.** Fuel has pooled in the intake port — this is what the engine encounters when a cracked insulator or leaking injector allows raw fuel to collect rather than reaching the cylinder as a calibrated mist. ### Cause 2 — Leaking Fuel Injector The fuel injector on a GY6 EFI engine is held in the intake manifold by two rubber O-rings (top and bottom). When these O-rings harden and crack with age, fuel weeps past the seal and drips into the intake port while the engine is at rest — the fuel rail remains pressurised for some time after the engine is switched off. Even a slow drip accumulates quickly enough to flood the cylinder overnight. A leaking injector body itself (cracked solenoid housing, degraded pintle seal) is less common but produces the same symptom. **Quick check:** Switch off the engine and wait 5 minutes. Remove the air intake duct and shine a torch into the throttle body bore. If you can see a wet sheen or fuel droplets on the port walls — and the engine has been off for several minutes — the injector is leaking past its seals. ## Tools & Parts Needed

## Step-by-Step Procedure ### Step 1 — Confirm Flooding and Clear the Cylinder 1. Turn the ignition off. On EFI engines the fuel pump stays primed — if possible, locate the fuel pump fuse and remove it to depressurise the rail before opening anything. 2. Remove the spark plug using a 16 mm plug socket. Inspect it: if it is wet and smells strongly of petrol, flooding is confirmed. 3. With the plug still out, hold the throttle fully open and crank the engine for 5–8 seconds (electric starter). This expels excess fuel from the cylinder as vapour. 4. Leave the plug out for 5–10 minutes to allow the cylinder to air out further. 5. Reinstall the spark plug (or a new one if the old plug is fuel-fouled). Tighten finger-tight plus one-quarter turn. **Test start now:** Reinstall the fuel pump fuse, turn the ignition on, wait for the pump prime cycle (2–3 seconds), then start. If it starts and runs normally, the flooding was a one-off event. If it floods again within minutes of stopping — there is an underlying leak to fix. ### Step 2 — Inspect the Intake Insulator 1. Remove the side panel or access cover to expose the throttle body. 2. Loosen both clamps securing the throttle body — the air duct side and the head-side insulator clamp. 3. Twist and pull the throttle body slightly away from the insulator to expose it. You do not need to disconnect all wiring harness connectors at this stage — just rotate it enough to see the insulator. 4. Squeeze and flex the insulator in all directions. Cracks often hide on the inner bore surface, along the top edge, or at the head-facing flange. Look for crazing, splits, or any visible gap. 5. CRACKED: Replace immediately — see Step 4. 6. INTACT: Refit the throttle body clamp. Proceed to Step 3 to check the injector. ### Step 3 — Inspect the Fuel Injector O-Rings 1. With the fuel pump fuse removed, fully disconnect the throttle body (harness connectors, throttle cable, coolant hoses if fitted). Set it on a clean rag. 2. Locate the fuel injector — it sits in a bore in the intake manifold or throttle body, held by a retaining clip or bracket. Release the clip and pull the injector straight out. 3. Inspect both O-rings on the injector body. They should be soft, uniformly round, and black. If they are flat, cracked, or shiny-hardened, they are no longer sealing. 4. Also inspect the injector body for fuel staining or wetness at the O-ring grooves — this confirms the leak path. 5. O-RINGS DEGRADED: Replace with a new O-ring kit — see Step 5. 6. INJECTOR BODY DAMAGED: Replace the entire injector — match the part number stamped on the injector body. 7. O-RINGS INTACT: Reinstall and check float height (not applicable — EFI). Re-examine for other causes such as a leaking fuel pressure regulator or a failed fuel pump check valve holding rail pressure after shutdown. ### Step 4 — Replace the Intake Insulator 1. Fully disconnect the throttle body (wiring harness, throttle cable, breather hoses) and set it aside. 2. Remove the two M6 nuts or bolts holding the insulator to the cylinder head studs. Use a 10 mm spanner or socket. 3. Pull the insulator free. Clean the cylinder head mating face — remove any old gasket material or debris. 4. Fit the new insulator. Ensure the paper or rubber gasket on the head-facing side is in place. Tighten the mounting nuts evenly to approximately 10 Nm — do not overtighten in the aluminium head. 5. Refit the throttle body into the insulator bore. Tighten both clamps firmly but not so tight that the clamp cuts into the rubber. 6. Reconnect all harness connectors, throttle cable, and hoses. **Do not use RTV silicone** on the intake insulator as a repair or seal. Silicone pieces can detach and enter the engine. Always replace with a new insulator. ### Step 5 — Replace the Injector O-Rings 1. Source an O-ring kit for your injector. Most GY6 EFI injectors use standard 14 mm × 1.5 mm and 11 mm × 1.5 mm Viton O-rings — confirm by measuring the old ones or searching your injector part number. 2. Lubricate the new O-rings lightly with clean engine oil before fitting — this prevents tearing on installation and ensures a proper seat. 3. Slide both O-rings onto the injector body into their respective grooves. 4. Push the injector squarely back into its bore in the manifold. It should seat without force — if it resists, check the O-ring is not folded or misaligned. 5. Refit the retaining clip or bracket so the injector cannot be pushed out by fuel pressure. 6. Reconnect the fuel rail and injector electrical connector. ### Step 6 — Verify the Repair 1. Reinstall the fuel pump fuse. Turn the ignition to ON (do not start) — you should hear the pump prime for 2–3 seconds. Wait 60 seconds and check around the injector and manifold for any fuel drips. 2. If no drips: start the engine and allow it to reach operating temperature (approximately 4–5 minutes). 3. Switch the engine off and wait 10 minutes. Remove the spark plug and confirm it is dry. Reinstall and start normally. 4. A cold start should now require just the normal key-on pump prime and one or two cranks. ## Troubleshooting Table

Poor grounding, corroded connectors, and misunderstood wiring configurations account for the majority of intermittent starting failures, charging issues, and lighting faults. This guide explains the GY6 electrical system architecture and provides a systematic diagnostic process. ## GY6 Electrical System Overview The GY6 uses a **magneto-based AC/DC charging system**. All modern GY6 scooters use a DC electrical system (battery-powered), but the stator generates AC current which the regulator/rectifier converts to regulated DC. There are two common ignition system configurations: #### AC CDI System Older configuration. CDI fires directly from AC current produced by the stator's pickup coil. Does not rely on battery voltage for spark. Common on pre-2010 GY6 50cc models. #### DC CDI System Modern configuration. CDI draws energy from the battery (12V DC). Requires a charged battery to fire spark. Standard on 125cc/150cc models and all Euro 4 variants. ## Key Electrical Components

Many BTC Riva, La Souris Sourini, and Santini Capri models use a nearly identical loom to the generic GY6 150cc Chinese scooter diagram. ## Systematic Fault Diagnosis ### Before You Start — Ground First Poor grounding is the single most common electrical fault on Chinese scooters. Before testing any component, do the following: 1. Locate the main ground point — usually a black wire bolted to the engine case or frame near the battery. 2. Unbolt it, clean the contact surface with sandpaper until shiny, and re-bolt firmly. 3. Inspect all black wire connectors in the loom. Clean or replace corroded connectors. 4. Check that the battery negative cable makes a solid connection to the frame. ### No Spark Diagnosis 1. **Check for spark:** Remove the spark plug. Reconnect the plug lead. Hold the plug against the engine case (ground). Crank the engine. You should see a strong blue spark. A weak yellow spark or no spark means a fault in the ignition chain. 2. **Check the kill switch:** Disconnect the kill switch wire from the CDI (usually the white/black wire). Try cranking again. If spark returns, the kill switch is shorted — clean or replace it. 3. **Check the sidestand switch:** Many GY6s cut ignition when the sidestand is down. Disconnect the sidestand switch and jump its two terminals together. If spark returns, the switch is faulty. 4. **Check CDI input voltage (DC CDI only):** With a multimeter, probe the red/battery wire on the CDI connector to ground. You should read 12V when the ignition is on. No voltage → check fuse and ignition switch. 5. **Test the pickup coil:** Disconnect the pickup coil from the CDI. Measure resistance across the two pickup coil wires with a multimeter. Typical specification is 80–150 Ω. Open circuit (infinite resistance) or short to ground means replace the stator assembly. 6. **Test the ignition coil primary:** Measure resistance between the coil's two primary terminals (where the CDI wire connects). Typical: 0.3–0.8 Ω. Test secondary (plug cap to ground): 5,000–15,000 Ω. Out-of-specification → replace coil. 7. **Substitute the CDI:** If all components test within specification but there is still no spark, the CDI itself is likely faulty. CDI units are inexpensive (€10–30); swap with a known-good unit to confirm. ### Charging System Diagnosis 1. **Battery voltage:** Measure battery voltage at rest (engine off, 15 minutes after last use). Healthy 12V AGM battery: 12.6–12.8V. Below 12.0V indicates a discharged or failing battery. 2. **Charging voltage:** Start the engine. Measure battery voltage with the engine running at ~3,500 RPM. Should read 13.8–14.5V. Above 15V indicates a failed regulator/rectifier (RR). Below 13.5V at speed indicates a weak stator or failed RR. 3. **Stator AC output:** Disconnect the stator yellow wire from the RR. With the engine running at 3,500 RPM, measure AC voltage between the yellow wire and engine ground. Should read 30–60V AC. Low output suggests a weak stator winding. 4. **RR diode test:** With a multimeter in diode test mode, test each diode leg of the rectifier section of the RR. A shorted diode (reads 0 in both directions) means replace the RR. ### Lighting Fault Diagnosis 1. **Headlight not working:** First check the main fuse and the dedicated headlight fuse/relay if fitted. Check for 12V at the headlight connector with ignition on. If voltage is present, the bulb is blown — replace with correct rating (typically 12V 35/35W halogen, BA20d base). 2. **Indicators flashing too fast or too slow:** Caused by mismatched bulb wattage or a failing flasher relay. Replace with standard 10W indicator bulbs and/or the flasher relay. 3. **Brake light not working:** Check both front (lever) and rear (pedal) brake light switches. Measure resistance across the switch — should read closed circuit (0 Ω) when brake is applied. Clean or adjust switch if sticking open. ## Essential Multimeter Tests at a Glance

The most problematic connectors to check are the main harness junction block (usually under the headset covers), the CDI connector, the RR connector (which handles high charging current and can melt if undersized), and the ignition switch connector.
